messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Carlos Hernandez still remembers the acrid taste of smoke and sweat that lingered in his mouth for days after the ambush. It was 1972, and he was a young soldier serving in Vietnam. His unit had been patrolling through a dense jungle when they were caught off guard by enemy fire. The chaos and confusion that followed are etched in his memory like scars. Carlos can recall the sound of gunfire and screams, the feeling of weightlessness as he fell to the ground, and the sensation of dizziness that washed over him as he struggled to get back up. Decades later, that same taste would transport Carlos back to those moments. He couldn't quite explain why, but whenever he encountered a specific type of cigar smoke or even certain types of spices, his stomach would drop, and he'd feel lightheaded. At first, it was just an occasional annoyance, something he learned to avoid by steering clear of certain situations or places. But over time, the association grew stronger, until the mere whiff of that smell could send him spiraling. Talking about the event itself wasn't much better. Carlos would often find himself glossing over details or changing the subject when asked about his time in Vietnam. He'd tried to explain it to friends and family before, but the words always seemed to get stuck in his throat. It was as if the memories themselves were too heavy to be spoken aloud. As a special education teacher, Carlos had learned to navigate complex emotions and challenging situations with ease. But he couldn't shake the feeling that certain environments or conversations might trigger those same feelings of overwhelm. He began to avoid situations that made him feel strong emotions – whether it was a heated discussion with colleagues or a particularly moving lesson plan. It wasn't that he didn't care; it's just that he'd come to believe that his own emotional well-being depended on maintaining a certain level of detachment. At school, Carlos developed the habit of sitting near exits and constantly scanning the room for signs of potential threats. His students might have seen him as vigilant or even overprotective, but for Carlos, these habits provided a sense of comfort in an uncertain world. He'd often find himself mentally mapping out escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere – whether it was a new classroom or a social gathering. Sounds, too, had become a source of hypervigilance for Carlos. Loud noises would make him jump; unexpected sounds would leave him on edge. His friends might tease him about being jumpy, but Carlos couldn't help the way his body responded to those stimuli. It was as if he'd developed an extra layer of skin that allowed him to sense even the smallest changes in his environment. Despite these efforts to stay safe, Carlos began to notice a change in himself over the years. He felt more and more disconnected from others – colleagues, friends, even his own students. Simple tasks, like grocery shopping or going out for dinner, had become daunting ordeals. His divorce several years prior had left him feeling isolated, but now he wondered if there was something deeper at play. One day, while teaching a lesson on emotional regulation to a group of rowdy teenagers, Carlos caught himself scanning the room with an unusual level of intensity. He realized that his own fears and avoidance behaviors had been shaping his interactions – not just with his students, but with everyone around him. It was this moment that brought him to seek help, a hesitant acknowledgment that perhaps it was time to confront the memories he'd spent so long avoiding. As Carlos sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands and glancing toward the door, he couldn't shake the feeling of vulnerability. He was most afraid of losing control – not just of his emotions but of his very surroundings. What frightened him most was the possibility that he'd never be able to fully shed the armor he'd built around himself. And yet, as he looked at the therapist with a mix of trepidation and hope, Carlos whispered a quiet admission: maybe it's time to try.
